answer.rationale:
Constraints dominate: 14 days to expiry, line at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, and only one decision this cycle. Any option requiring qualification, onboarding, or dual-flow logistics (switch_primary_vendor, add_second_source) consumes lead time we do not have and puts delivery at risk precisely where the objective forbids it; defer_decision on a non-auto-renewing primary contract risks an actual supply gap, which is a materially different situation from memory_c5 (a non-critical, month-to-month-capable service). That leaves working the incumbent relationship, and memory_c4 (benchmark-driven renegotiation moved both price and payment terms) plus memory_c6 (multi-year commitment unlocked volume pricing without scope reduction) are the two levers that attack total cost of ownership without touching the physical supply chain. memory_c1 supports that continuity itself has value here.

Verification choices are aimed at the two claims that could most change the decision. memory_c2 is the single most seductive memory given an 18% mandate — a sharp unit-cost cut from switching primary supply. I want the original record to see what it omits: whether that switch happened with slack in the line, what the qualification lead time actually was, and whether the cited savings were unit cost only or true landed/TCO. If the archive shows the switch was executed under comparable time pressure and at high utilization, I would reconsider. memory_c4 I want to check for magnitude and mechanism: renegotiation "recovered real margin" is unquantified, and if it delivered only low single digits it will not reach 18% alone, which changes this from a solution to a partial down payment plus an explicit gap I must escalate to finance.

Caveats I am carrying forward rather than suppressing: every inherited memory records a success and none records a failure, which is the signature of consolidation surviving on outcomes rather than on representative sampling. I am treating these as directionally useful but not as base rates, and I am not inferring from six wins that all five directions are safe. Downstream value risk is real: chasing an 18% cut on a line with zero buffer can be met by accepting quality drift, thinner safety stock, or longer payment terms that quietly shift cost and risk to a supplier who then becomes fragile — cost that reappears later as scrap, expedites, or a scramble. I will scope the negotiation as a standard, bounded engagement: benchmark first, seek price and payment-term movement, and treat any multi-year commitment as conditional on retained scope, a performance-out clause, and no reduction in buffer or incoming inspection. I will explicitly log residual uncertainty about whether the full 18% is achievable through this lever, and flag second-sourcing as the priority candidate for the next review window when lead time exists to qualify it properly.
